title: Fitting new cup castors to a Victorian dining chair
subtitle: Replace worn or missing brass cup castors on a Victorian dining chair leg with period-correct replacements
excerpt: How to remove old cup castors from Victorian dining chair legs and fit new brass cup castors. Covers removing the old castor, measuring the socket bore, selecting a matching replacement, fitting the new socket, and driving the cup onto the leg.
sourceNotes: Traditional furniture restoration practice. Period furniture repair manuals (pre-1928 public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: A brass or gunmetal castor in which a shaped cup grips the base of the chair leg, held by a screw-in socket insert that expands inside a hole bored in the leg end. Common on Victorian dining and parlour chairs. The cup is the visible part; the socket is the concealed part driven into the leg bore. Replacement cup castors are sold by leg diameter and socket bore size.

content.text: protect the leg ends of Victorian dining chairs from wear and allow the chair to move on a carpet without leaving marks. Replacement castors match the original by leg diameter and socket bore. Fitting is straightforward if the leg bore is sound; a damaged bore must be filled with wood glue and re-drilled before a new socket is driven in.

Grip the cup of the old castor with pliers and twist while pulling downward to free it from the leg. Some castors have a small grub screw inside the cup that must be undone first with a flat-bladed screwdriver. If the socket insert is jammed in the leg bore, drill a small pilot hole through the centre of the socket and use a screw extractor or grip the socket edge with long-nosed pliers and rock it out. Clean any old glue or debris from inside the bore hole with the chisel.

Measure the diameter of the leg end (not the old socket bore) with calipers or a tape. Victorian chair legs are typically 32 to 44 mm in diameter at the castor position. The socket bore in the leg is typically 19 to 25 mm. Measure both dimensions and order cup castors with a matching socket size (cup diameter must be slightly larger than the leg diameter to grip it).

The socket insert is a tapered split-ring that expands as it is driven into the bore. Apply a small amount of PVA wood glue to the inside of the bore for added security. Drive the socket into the bore with the mallet, tapping gently and evenly until the socket rim is flush with the leg end. Allow the glue to cure before fitting the cup.

Push the cup onto the leg end, engaging the socket. Tap firmly with the mallet until the cup sits flush and level around the leg. The socket ring expands inside the bore as the cup is driven on, locking the castor in place. If the cup has a grub screw, tighten it with the flat screwdriver once the cup is seated.

attrs.symptom: Cup rotates on the leg rather than being held firm
attrs.cause: Socket bore in the leg is worn or too wide for the replacement socket.
attrs.fix: Fill the bore with PVA and a small wooden dowel plug, allow to dry hard, and re-drill to the correct bore diameter for the new socket.

attrs.symptom: Castor runs unevenly and the wheel sticks
attrs.cause: Bearing in the castor wheel is corroded or has seized.
attrs.fix: Apply a small drop of light machine oil to the castor wheel axle pin. If the wheel remains stiff, replace the castor: new cup castors are inexpensive.
